title: TECHNIQUES FOR USING MACHINE LEARNING TO TEST INTEGRATED CIRCUIT DIES
technical_field: The present disclosure relates generally to the field of integrated circuit (IC) testing and, more specifically, to techniques for using machine learning (ML) models to predict IC die failures during the manufacturing process.
background_art: Configurable integrated circuits (ICs) are configured by users to implement custom logic functions. A logic designer uses computer-aided design (CAD) tools to design a custom circuit. Upon completion, the CAD tools generate an image containing configuration data bits, which are loaded into configuration memory elements to configure the ICs to perform the custom circuit functions. Integrated circuit (IC) dies are typically tested before being used on customer circuit boards. Bench testing of IC dies coupled to customer circuit boards can identify marginal IC dies. However, in high-volume manufacturing (HVM) of transceiver IC dies, external loopback transceiver screening may be insufficient to screen marginal IC dies compared to bench testing. ICs that pass HVM tests may still fail certain protocols on bench or in customer setups, indicating a gap in the screening process. Identifying the root cause of these failures and implementing a fix is a significant and costly undertaking.
summary_of_invention: The present disclosure provides techniques for using machine learning (ML) models to predict integrated circuit (IC) die failures during the manufacturing process. A computing system includes a processor circuit configured to receive test data generated from testing IC dies in a test flow. The computing system includes an ML model that uses this test data to predict bench results, which are indicative of which IC dies fail to satisfy a manufacturing protocol when coupled to circuit boards. This approach enables accurate prediction of bench failures, improving the efficiency and effectiveness of IC testing and reducing defects.

detailed_description:
The disclosure describes techniques for using machine learning (ML) models to predict integrated circuit (IC) die failures during manufacturing. Integrated circuit (IC) dies are typically tested before use on customer circuit boards. Bench testing of IC dies coupled to customer circuit boards can identify marginal IC dies. However, in high-volume manufacturing (HVM) of transceiver IC dies, external loopback transceiver screening may be insufficient to screen marginal IC dies compared to bench testing. IC dies that pass HVM tests may still fail certain protocols on bench or in customer setups, indicating a gap in the screening process. Identifying the root cause of these failures and implementing a fix is a significant and costly undertaking.

According to some examples, an ML model (e.g., an XGBoost algorithm) is trained on data from bench-failing IC dies coupled to circuit boards to predict bench fallout during the manufacturing process. The ML model uses gradient-boosted decision trees and is constructed using HVM sort and class logged parameters along with bench data, enabling accurate prediction of bench failures when IC dies are coupled to customer circuit boards.

Multiple ML models (e.g., six models) can be developed for external loopback testing. When combined, these ML models can predict 100% of bench fallouts. These techniques can be applied to all types of analog and digital circuits, including transceiver IC dies and digital circuits like static random access memory (SRAM) IC dies.

FIG. 1 illustrates a flow chart for incorporating ML models into IC manufacturing. A regular manufacturing process produces IC dies. In operation 101, these dies are subjected to sort and class locations. In operation 102, ML models are run in the background using data from a database to generate prediction outputs for each lot and wafer. In operation 103, test data is updated with these ML prediction outputs. Rejected IC dies can be saved for potential use after a firmware fix.

XGBoost, or Extreme Gradient Boosting, is an advanced ML implementation effective for predicting IC die failures on bench tests. It offers features like regularization, parallel computation, and handling sparse data, making it faster, more scalable, and more accurate than traditional gradient boosting methods.

FIG. 2 details the process of training an ML model. This includes importing libraries (201), initializing and loading data (202), performing data preprocessing (203), encoding categorical features (204), scaling data (205), splitting data into features and target variables (206), training a classifier with specific parameters and adjusting for class imbalances (207), saving the trained model and extracting feature importance (208), generating predictions and evaluating performance (209), saving predictions and related reports (210), and generating visualizations of feature importances (211).

FIG. 3 outlines a flow chart for identifying IC dies that fail a manufacturing protocol using a trained ML model. This involves importing and preprocessing test data (301), applying a scaler for normalization (302), using the trained ML model to predict passing or failing dies (303), evaluating predictions against known failing dies (304), and generating a summary of prediction results and yields (305).

FIG. 4 presents another flow chart for identifying IC dies that fail a manufacturing protocol. Operations include importing libraries (401), defining helper functions (402), loading and concatenating test data (403), preprocessing data (404), encoding categorical features (405), scaling data (406), splitting data into features and target outputs (407), loading the trained ML model (408), generating prediction probabilities and binary outcomes (409), saving predictions (410), calculating metrics for passing dies (411), and calculating and summarizing passing rates and yields (412).

FIG. 5 illustrates an example of a configurable logic integrated circuit (IC) 500, which may represent one of the IC dies tested. It includes configurable functional blocks like LABs 510, RAM 530, and DSP 520, along with input/output elements (IOEs) 502 and programmable interconnect circuitry.

FIG. 6A shows a system 10 for implementing a circuit design on a programmable logic device 19 using design software 14 and a compiler 16 to generate a bitstream 18.

FIG. 6B depicts a programmable logic device 19 with fabric die 22 and base die 24 connected via microbumps 26.

FIG. 7 illustrates a computing system 700 with a processing subsystem 70 and an I/O subsystem 50, which can implement the disclosed embodiments.
claims: A computing system comprising: at least one processor circuit configured to receive first test data generated from testing integrated circuit dies in a test flow, wherein the computing system comprises a machine learning model that uses the first test data generated from the test flow to predict bench results that are indicative of which ones of the integrated circuit dies fail to satisfy a manufacturing protocol when the integrated circuit dies are coupled to circuit boards.
The computing system of claim 1, wherein the computing system uses the machine learning model to reduce defects in the integrated circuit dies coupled to the circuit boards.

The computing system of claim 1, wherein the computing system is further configured to encode second test data generated from testing the integrated circuit dies by converting categorical string values in the second test data into numerical values in the first test data.

The computing system of claim 1, wherein the computing system is further configured to scale second test data generated from testing the integrated circuit dies by normalizing the second test data to generate the first test data.

The computing system of claim 1, wherein the computing system is further configured to determine if the first test data has more parameters than the machine learning model is using and to remove any of the parameters in the first test data that the machine learning model is not using.
The computing system of claim 1, wherein the bench results comprise transceiver or serializer/deserializer links.

The computing system of claim 1, wherein the computing system is further configured to adjust thresholds of the machine learning model to affect predictions of the bench results, and wherein the computing system is further configured to evaluate results of the predictions of the bench results across different ones of the thresholds to optimize performance of the machine learning model.

The computing system of claim 1, wherein the computing system is further configured to train the machine learning model to identify additional integrated circuit dies that fail to satisfy the manufacturing protocol using training data generated from the additional integrated circuit dies.
The computing system of claim 1, wherein the computing system is further configured to use an Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) model to predict the bench results.

A method for predicting if integrated circuit dies fail a manufacturing protocol, the method comprising: receiving first test data generated from testing the integrated circuit dies in a test flow at a computing system comprising at least one processor circuit; and using a machine learning model running on the computing system to generate predictions of bench results based on the first test data input to the machine learning model, wherein the bench results are indicative of which of the integrated circuit dies fail to satisfy the manufacturing protocol when the integrated circuit dies are coupled to circuit boards.
The method of claim 10 further comprising: using the machine learning model to reduce defects in the integrated circuit dies coupled to the circuit boards.
The method of claim 10, wherein the bench results comprise transceiver or serializer/deserializer links.

The method of claim 10 further comprising: adjusting thresholds of the machine learning model to affect the predictions using the computing system; and evaluating results of the predictions across different ones of the thresholds using the computing system to optimize performance of the machine learning model.
The method of claim 10 further comprising: scaling second test data generated from testing the integrated circuit dies by normalizing the second test data to generate the first test data.

The method of claim 10, wherein using the machine learning model running on the computing system to generate the predictions of the bench results further comprises using an Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) model running on the computing system to generate the predictions of the bench results.

A non-transitory computer readable storage medium comprising computer readable instructions stored thereon for causing a computing system to: receive training data generated based on testing first integrated circuit dies at the computing system comprising at least one processor circuit; train a machine learning model using the computing system by comparing outputs of the machine learning model generated with the training data to first bench results for the first integrated circuit dies, wherein the first bench results indicate the first integrated circuits dies that fail a manufacturing protocol when the first integrated circuit dies are coupled to first circuit boards; and generate predictions of second bench results for second integrated circuit dies using the machine learning model running on the computing system based on test data generated from testing the second integrated circuit dies, wherein the second bench results indicate the second integrated circuit dies that fail the manufacturing protocol when the second integrated circuit dies are coupled to second circuit boards.

The non-transitory computer readable storage medium of claim 16, wherein the computer readable instructions further cause the computing system to: adjust for class imbalances using different sample weights for the machine learning model using the computing system if the machine learning model generates an imbalance in the second integrated circuit dies that fail the manufacturing protocol compared to the second integrated circuit dies that pass the manufacturing protocol.

The non-transitory computer readable storage medium of claim 16, wherein the computer readable instructions further cause the computing system to: extract top features of the machine learning model using the computing system based on feature importance that indicates which input parameters to the machine learning model are most affecting the outputs of the machine learning model.

The non-transitory computer readable storage medium of claim 16, wherein the computer readable instructions further cause the computing system to: generate the predictions using features for the test data with the machine learning model without the second bench results; and compare the predictions to the second bench results for the second integrated circuit dies to determine if the predictions match the second bench results to generate a capture rate.

The non-transitory computer readable storage medium of claim 16, wherein the computer readable instructions further cause the computing system to: generate the predictions of the second bench results for the second integrated circuit dies that fail at least two manufacturing protocols based on the test data using the machine learning model, wherein the manufacturing protocols comprise at least two of Long Range, Very Short Range, and Chip-to-Module.
abstract: A computing system includes a processor circuit configured to receive test data generated from testing integrated circuit dies in a test flow. The computing system includes a machine learning model that uses the test data generated from the test flow to predict bench results that are indicative of which ones of the integrated circuit dies fail to satisfy a manufacturing protocol when the integrated circuit dies are coupled to circuit boards.
